noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: describe the differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration
know the word equation and the balanced chemical symbol equation for aerobic respiration in living organisms
know the word equation for anaerobic respiration in plants and in animals

primer.text: Cells never sit idle: every process they run, from pumping ions to contracting fibres, has to be paid for in energy. This note walks through how glucose is cashed in — completely, with oxygen, or partially without it — and why the two routes differ so much in their yield and their waste products.

lessons.title: Aerobic Respiration
lessons.opening: Aerobic respiration is the oxygen-powered route: nutrient molecules are broken down completely inside the mitochondria, transferring a large amount of energy into ATP while carbon dioxide and water leave as the only wastes.
keyPoints: Aerobic means the process needs oxygen and happens in the mitochondria.
Glucose is broken down completely, so the energy yield is large.
The waste products are carbon dioxide and water.
Plant and animal cells alike run this pathway around the clock.

low.restatement: With oxygen present, cells split glucose fully inside mitochondria, giving plenty of ATP plus carbon dioxide and water.
low.analogy: An open fire with plenty of air: complete burning, lots of heat, little left over but ash.
low.examPointer: Quote the definition faithfully: oxygen, nutrient breakdown, ATP release.

medium.restatement: Oxygen lets the enzymes oxidise glucose all the way, so almost every usable joule ends up captured in ATP.
medium.analogy: A full salary versus a part-payment: the aerobic route collects everything the glucose can offer.
medium.examPointer: When asked why the yield is large, answer 'complete breakdown', not merely 'oxygen present'.

check.stem: Where in a cell does aerobic respiration mainly take place?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The nucleus stores genetic instructions; it is not where glucose is broken down.
Ribosomes assemble proteins rather than releasing energy.
The membrane manages what enters and leaves, not energy release.

check.stem: Which substances leave aerobic respiration as waste products?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Lactic acid belongs to the oxygen-free pathway in animal cells.
That pair comes from yeast respiring without oxygen.
These are the inputs consumed, not the outputs released.

check.stem: Why does the aerobic route release more energy from one glucose molecule?

options.text: The glucose is broken down completely, so far fewer usable bonds remain unharvested
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because oxygen itself is a fuel
options.explanation: Oxygen enables the oxidation; it is not an energy source on its own.

options.text: Because mitochondria multiply during the process
options.explanation: Organelle numbers are not what raises the yield.

options.text: Because carbon dioxide stores the spare energy
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a low-energy waste, not a store.

check.stem: Which statement about aerobic respiration is true for plant roots at midnight?

options.text: Root cells keep running it because every living cell needs ATP around the clock
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It stops because photosynthesis has stopped
options.explanation: Respiration runs independently of photosynthesis in the dark.

options.text: It switches to using sunlight directly
options.explanation: Cells cannot power reactions with raw sunlight.
Every living plant cell, roots included, respires.

check.stem: What does aerobic respiration hand to the cell for it to spend?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Glucose is the fuel consumed, not the currency released.
Oxygen is consumed as the oxidant.
Proteins are a nutrient class, not the energy currency here.

check.stem: State the word equation for the aerobic breakdown of glucose.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water, with energy transferred to ATP.

check.stem: Name the organelle where aerobic respiration happens and the gas it consumes.
check.modelAnswer: It happens in the mitochondria and consumes oxygen.

check.stem: Explain why aerobic respiration transfers more energy than the oxygen-free route.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen allows the complete oxidation of glucose, so almost all the bond energy is harvested into ATP, whereas partial breakdown leaves energy locked in the products.

check.stem: A jogger's leg muscles carry on aerobic respiration throughout a steady run. Describe what the cells take in and give out.
check.modelAnswer: They take in oxygen and glucose, break the glucose down completely inside mitochondria, and release carbon dioxide and water while transferring energy into ATP for contraction.

lessons.title: The Aerobic Equations in Both Forms
lessons.opening: The aerobic pathway is written two ways: a word equation naming each substance, and a balanced chemical equation showing exactly one glucose reacting with six oxygen molecules to give six carbon dioxide and six water molecules.
keyPoints: Word form: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
The symbol equation must be balanced for full credit.
One glucose consumes six oxygen molecules.

low.restatement: Learn the word version first, then the balanced symbol one with the sixes attached.
low.analogy: A recipe in plain language versus the exact weighed quantities on a chemist's sheet.
low.examPointer: If the question says 'balanced symbol equation', words alone score nothing.

medium.restatement: Balancing works because each glucose holds six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens, so six O2, six CO2 and six H2O conserve every atom.
medium.analogy: Atom bookkeeping: nothing may appear or vanish, only be rearranged.
medium.examPointer: Practise writing the symbol version from memory; the balance check earns the marks.

check.stem: How many oxygen molecules react with one glucose molecule in the balanced aerobic equation?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Four oxygens would leave the atom count unbalanced.
Twelve doubles what the equation requires.
Two is far too few to oxidise one glucose fully.

check.stem: What is the correct symbol equation for aerobic respiration?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That runs the opposite way and describes photosynthesis.
Oxygen is missing; the aerobic route cannot run without it.
The reactants and products are swapped around.

check.stem: Which substances sit on the right-hand side of the aerobic symbol equation?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Those are the reactants on the left.
Ethanol belongs to fermentation, not this route.
Lactic acid is the animal oxygen-free product.

check.stem: A student answers a 'balanced symbol equation' question using words only. What follows?

options.text: No credit, because the command word demands chemical formulas
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Full credit if the words are in the right order
options.explanation: The mark scheme requires the symbols themselves.
Schemes do not award partial marks for the wrong form.

options.text: Credit once the spelling is correct
options.explanation: Spelling does not substitute for the required formulas.

check.stem: Why must the symbol equation be balanced?

options.text: Atoms are conserved, so every atom entering must appear among the products
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: To make the equation look longer
options.explanation: Length has nothing to do with validity.

options.text: Because oxygen always comes in sixes
options.explanation: The sixes follow from conservation, not habit.

options.text: So that energy can be shown
options.explanation: Energy is not part of the balancing rule.

check.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration.
State how many carbon dioxide molecules form from one glucose molecule.
check.modelAnswer: Six carbon dioxide molecules form for every glucose respired aerobically.

check.stem: Explain why answering with words alone is risky when the question asks for a symbol equation.
check.modelAnswer: Because the command word requires chemical formulas, and only the formulas carry the atom counts that balancing proves.

check.stem: A classmate writes C6H12O6 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. Correct the line and justify your edit.
check.modelAnswer: Insert the sixes: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O, since one glucose needs six oxygens and yields six of each product, keeping atoms conserved.

lessons.title: Going Without Oxygen in Animals
lessons.opening: When muscles demand energy faster than the blood can deliver oxygen, they switch on the oxygen-free pathway: glucose is only partially broken down, a little ATP is transferred, and lactic acid accumulates as the leftover product.
keyPoints: The oxygen-free route needs no oxygen at all.
Glucose breakdown is incomplete, so the ATP yield is small.
Animal muscle cells make lactic acid during vigorous exercise.
Lactic acid lowers tissue pH and can disturb enzymes.
Leftover lactic acid is later oxidised using oxygen.

low.restatement: No oxygen, small payout, lactic acid left behind in the muscles.
low.analogy: Pawning a watch: cash arrives fast, but much of the value stays unclaimed until you buy it back.
low.examPointer: The animal word equation is glucose to lactic acid; no symbol version is required.

medium.restatement: Insufficient oxygen delivery forces the partial route, so energy stays trapped in the lactic acid bonds while the tissue turns acidic.
medium.analogy: A fire starved of air leaves charred half-burnt wood: the fuel was never fully consumed.
medium.examPointer: Link the pH drop to enzyme shape: acidic conditions can denature proteins and slow recovery.

check.stem: What builds up in hard-working muscle cells when oxygen runs short?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Yeast makes ethanol; animal cells do not.
Carbon dioxide dominates the aerobic route, not this one.
Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate, not the waste here.

check.stem: How does the energy yield of the oxygen-free route compare, per glucose?

options.text: Much smaller, because the breakdown stops partway
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Larger, since glucose is handled faster
options.explanation: Speed does not raise the yield; completeness does.
The incomplete split leaves energy behind.

options.text: Zero, because no oxygen is used
options.explanation: A little ATP is still transferred.

check.stem: Why can sustained lactic acid accumulation harm performance?

options.text: It lowers muscle pH, and acidic conditions can denature enzymes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: It raises muscle pH, blocking nerves
options.explanation: The shift is toward acidity, not alkalinity.
Membranes do not melt; enzymes lose their shape.
The acid is later broken down using oxygen, not bound by it.

check.stem: Which word equation describes the oxygen-free pathway in animal cells?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
That is the plant and yeast version.
Oxygen is absent from this route by definition.
Those are the aerobic products.

check.stem: During a sprint, why do muscle cells still run some aerobic respiration?

options.text: Oxygen supply persists but cannot fully match demand, so both routes run side by side
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The aerobic route shuts down entirely in sprints
options.explanation: It continues, contributing most of the steady ATP.

options.text: The oxygen-free route replaces it completely
options.explanation: Both operate; the second tops up the shortfall.

options.text: Muscles stop needing energy at high intensity
options.explanation: Demand rises, which is exactly why both engage.

check.stem: State the fate of lactic acid once exercise ends.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen breaks the lactic acid down into carbon dioxide and water.

check.stem: Name the compound whose partial breakdown defines the animal oxygen-free route.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose is only partially broken down, leaving lactic acid.

check.stem: Explain why the oxygen-free route transfers only a little ATP per glucose.
check.modelAnswer: Because glucose is not fully oxidised; energy remains stored in the lactic acid molecules that leave the pathway.

check.stem: A swimmer's shoulders ache near the end of a race. Use both respiration routes to explain the ache.
check.modelAnswer: Sustained effort outpaces oxygen delivery, so the muscles add the oxygen-free route and produce lactic acid; its build-up lowers the tissue pH, and that acidic environment is sensed as the ache.

lessons.title: Plants, Yeast and the Head-to-Head Comparison
sourceHeadings: Anaerobic respiration in plants and fungi
lessons.opening: Plant and yeast cells take the oxygen-free route to a different destination: glucose breaks down into ethanol and carbon dioxide, and in yeast this fermentation is harnessed by bakers, while the comparison table sets the two routes side by side.
keyPoints: Plants and yeast produce ethanol and carbon dioxide without oxygen.
The oxygen-free breakdown in yeast is called fermentation.
Bread-making exploits the carbon dioxide from fermentation.
Aerobic gives a lot of ATP; the oxygen-free route gives a little.
Oxygen use and waste products are the key contrast points.

low.restatement: Without oxygen, plants and yeast make ethanol plus carbon dioxide, and far less ATP.
low.analogy: Two campsites: one runs a full stove (oxygen), the other packs a snack — both feed you, one much better.
low.examPointer: Learn the yeast equation: glucose to ethanol plus carbon dioxide.

medium.restatement: The comparison rests on four axes: oxygen demand, completeness of breakdown, waste products and the amount of ATP transferred.
medium.analogy: Compare runners by distance covered: one finishes the whole race, the other stops halfway.
medium.examPointer: Table questions reward precise pairs: lactic acid for animals, ethanol plus carbon dioxide for plants and yeast.

check.stem: Which products form when yeast respire without oxygen?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Animal cells make lactic acid; yeast does not.
Oxygen is a reactant in the aerobic route, never a product here.
Neither belongs to any respiration pathway.

check.stem: What is fermentation?

options.text: The oxygen-free breakdown of glucose by yeast
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Any breakdown of glucose in leaves
options.explanation: The term is tied to yeast and similar fungi.
Bread uses fermentation, but fermentation itself needs no oxygen.

options.text: The conversion of starch into glucose
options.explanation: That is digestion, not fermentation.

check.stem: In bread-making, which fermentation product lifts the dough?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Ethanol evaporates during baking; it does not raise the dough.
Water is not the raising agent.
ATP powers the yeast cells, not the expansion of the dough.

check.stem: Which row of a respiration comparison table is stated correctly?

options.text: Oxygen used: aerobic yes, oxygen-free no
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Aerobic is the complete one.
Lactic acid versus ethanol and carbon dioxide differ.
The oxygen-free yield is smaller.

check.stem: Why does the oxygen-free route in plants leave ethanol behind?

options.text: The glucose is only partly broken down, so carbon and energy stay in the ethanol
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Ethanol is a store the plant reuses for photosynthesis
options.explanation: It is a waste of this route, not a fuel store.
The two simply coexist as products.

options.text: Plants lack mitochondria for full breakdown
options.explanation: Plant cells have mitochondria; the route differs because oxygen is absent.

check.stem: State the word equation for the oxygen-free route in yeast.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose gives ethanol and carbon dioxide.

check.stem: Name one industry example that relies on fermentation.
check.modelAnswer: Bread-making relies on the carbon dioxide released by yeast fermentation.

check.stem: Explain why the two routes share one comparison table yet produce different wastes.
check.modelAnswer: Because the presence or absence of oxygen decides how far glucose is oxidised, and each stopping point defines a different waste product.

check.stem: A baker notices dough rising faster in a warm kitchen. Explain the biology behind the observation.
check.modelAnswer: Warmth speeds yeast fermentation, so more carbon dioxide is released per minute, inflating the dough quicker.

glossary.definition: The organelles where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose.
The energy-transfer molecule that cells spend to power their processes.
The partial-breakdown product made by animal cells short of oxygen.
The oxygen-free breakdown of glucose by yeast, harnessed in baking.
